Hon. J. D. REID (Acting Minister of Railways and Canals) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 122, to amend the Government Railways Small Claims Act.
He said: There is an Act on the statute book under the provisions of which the Government Railways Managing Board is the defendant on any suit entered against the Intercolonial railway. This Bill is simply for the purpose of substituting the words ' General Manager of Government Railways ' for the words ' Government Railways Managing Board,' making the General Manager of Government Railways the defendant instead of the Government Railways Managing Board.
Is it a very good practice to make a general manager the defendant?

The Government Railways
Managing Board is not now in existence.

I know. If the Department of Justice thinks that the proper way to amend the Act, I have no objection to offer. The Ontario Legislature has refused to pass a Bill of this character with reference to small claims, and compels the claimants to sue the Crown, as was originally the course followed in the Dominion Parliament.	'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not suppose it is
intended to call the defendant by name; he will be sued in his capacity as General Manager of the Intercolonial.
Representing the Crown?
It is a matter of procedure mostly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Entirely. The Act at present on the statute book provides this inexpensive way of testing claims against the Intercolonial railway, which otherwise would have to go into the Exchequer Court.

Is it intended to
change?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, there is no .change in the existing procedure except that, as a matter of form, the words, 'general manager of the Intercolonial railway' are substituted for the words 'Government Railways Managing Board.'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: 1. It is not easy to give a definition in each case, as there may in certain cases be an overlapping. Speaking generally, however, oommeraial fish are those that are caught iby regular fishermen as a means of livelihood, while sporting fish are those that are caught by sportsmen for pastime or pleasure. The principal sporting fish in Ontario are speckled trout and black bass.

2. Since the 1898 Privy Council decision in the Fisheries Reference, the fisheries of Ontario have been supervised by the provincial Government. Last year an arrangement was made with the provincial Department of Fisheries-which received the revenue from the fisheries-whereby the Department of Marine and Fisheries will confine its fish breeding operations to the stocking of waters resorted to by regular fishermen to earn their livelihood, while the provincial department will attend to the stocking of the sport fishing waters of the province.

On the motion of the Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) for Committee of Supply :
Mr. GEO. E. McCRANEY (Saskatoon): I would like to cal] the attention
4 p.m. of the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) to an article which appeared in the Saskatoon Daily Star of March 5 last, headed, 'Are Homesteads Taxed Illegally in Saskatchewan?' My apology for taking up the time of the House on this subject is the fact that this article, and the correspondence which has ensued in consequence of it, have attracted considerable attention in the province of iSaskatehewan, and my purpose in bringing it to the attention of the minister is to obtain from him a statement as to the position of the Department of the Interior on the matter. The article to which I refer is as follows;

Are Homesteaders Taxed Illegally in Saskatchewan?-Department Official Says Land is Exempt Until Government Releases Title-Saskatchewan Government and Municipalities who are Taxing all Occupied Lands are Affected.
The question was sprung upon a Star man today:	' Can municipalities or even the provincial Government, legally tax land, the title to which has not passed out of the hands ot the Crown, or federal Government?'
The reason for the query was a recent declaration within the Department of the Interior that such lands, until patent Is transferred to the occupant or purchaser, are exempt from municipal and school taxation, etc. The letter is from an official of the department and reads in part:
I am just in receipt of a communication from the department stating that they have received several complaints against municipal councils throughout the province of Saskatchewan levying taxes on unpatented homesteads, and stating that the same is illegal. .	.	.
The department has written a letter to the municipal commissioner of the province of Saskatchewan directing his attention to the matter, and pointing out that it is clearly illegal for municipal, school or other local authorities to levy taxes on unpatented lands. Our department is anxious to get a list of the municipalities that are doing this work so that it can take the matter up with the Minister of Justice in order to have this illegal practice stopped at once.
Is the Taxing Illegal?
The letter just quoted from is of the utmost significance. For instance, in the municipality of Cory, which surrounds this city, practically no distinction is made, a Star man was given to understand to-day upon inquiry at the municipality's office on Twentieth street, just west of the Y.M.C.A. building, whether the land taxed is held under patent by the occupant or if the title is still in the possession of the Dominion Government.
According to the letter a homesteader's land is exempted until he. receives his patent. The homesteader has, however, been taxed right along by the municipality for years before he came into possession of the patent to the land. If it can be established that such taxing was illegal it is conceivable that Cory may be called upon to refund immense sums of money. There is instance after instance where the homesteader has been made to pay taxes for anywhere from three to six years when, assuming that the letter quoted from is correct he could not legally be taxed. In one case mentioned to the Star to-day, a man was actually forced off his land because of inability to pay the taxes. And this has been going on throughout the whole province.
What About the Provincial Government?
Has the provincial Government along with the municipalities been collecting thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars to which they are not legally entitled?
The point is a decidedly interesting one and should be put to the test of the courts, said a prominent barrister of the city before whom the matter was laid to-day for an opinion. He cited the case of a man who had bought Dominion Government school lands and was taxed by the Cory municipality from the date of his purchase notwithstanding that the title to the property continued to remain in the possession of the Government for a long time
until paid for. As Government land it was exempt from taxation and the purchaser applied for a refund on this ground, but was informed that the provincial Government gave authority to impose the tax. He did not proceed with his suit. The point, then is, has the provincial Government the authority to give such permission and is itself not guilty of illegal practice in levying toll from exempted land?
The practice has been for municipalities to get after the homesteader, as soon as he registers his claim to a piece of homestead land and clap on all the taxes to which he would be liable as the owner outright of the property. Both municipal and provincial taxes are exacted right up to the time he receives his patent, and after, of course. The taxing even extends to grazing leases, where settlers obtain rights to use Government land, but take no steps to gain title.
Now a Government official declares that lands, the title to which is still with the Government, are exempt. If the ruling becomes official the revenues of the municipalities and the provincial treasury will be enormously reduced, and it might even mean, said one today, the refunding of millions of dollars.
I have read the whole article, which appears in the Saskatoon Daily Star, the Conservative newspaper in the city of Saskatoon. The letter quoted is said by the Saskatoon Daily Star in another issue to have been written by a prominent official of the department on the departmental letterhead. Its conclusions as to the right of the province or the municipalities to tax homesteaders are so astonishing that I think it advisable to call the attention of the minister to them, and to obtain from him a statement as to whether the department acquiesces in this expression'of opinion by one of its officials, or whether the department holds otherwise.
There is no doubt as to what view the Saskatoon Daily Star takes of this letter. I will read one sentence again:
According to the letter a homesteader's land is exempt until he receives his patent.
That would mean that no homesteaders are subject to taxation in the province of Saskatchewan. In Saskatchewan our understanding has always been that lands vested in the Crown are not taxable nor are lands in which the Crown is interested as a beneficiary owner. But it has been the practice, and I believe legally so, that the interest of a homesteader in a homestead should be the subject of taxation.
There has been some correspondence between Mr. Pereira of the Department of the Interior and the Deputy Minister of Municipal Affairs of Saskatchewan with regard to another matter. Mr. Pereira, in his letter, dated the I6th of February, 1914, draws the attention of the Department of Municipal Affairs to the fact that some of our muni-

cipalities are allowing taxes to stand against homesteads which have been abandoned or cancelled, so that homesteaders, who presumably receive free grants from the Government, take them subject to some taxes placed against them, when other persons have been in occupation of them. So far as that point taken by Mr. Pereira is concerned, it is one upon which we all agree-that there is no right in the province or in the municipalities to create a lien upon any homestead belonging to the Crown. The letter, however, mentioned in the Saskatoon Daily Star, in the article which I have quoted is not the letter of Mr. Pereira to the Department of Municipal Affairs; and when one compares them, one will see that the views are altogether different. Mr. Pereira's view is in accord with that of the Department of Municipal Affairs, who say that they are doing all they can to prevent these taxes which are levied against homesteads, from being levied against homesteads which have been abandoned or cancelled. The fact that any official of the department should write any such letter carries considerable consequences with it. Such a letter, with a declaration as to the right of the province to tax homestead lands, can have no legal effect. What any servant of the department may think, or what may be the official view of the department, can have no effect in law, because the law is not interpreted by the department, but by the judges of the land. The only result which such an expression of opinion by an official of the department and its publication in one of the leading papers of the province can have, is to disturb the public mind and to cause trouble, because it is not desirable that any false views should be spread throughout the province as to the liability of those in possession of homestead lands to be taxed for them.
My purpose in bringing this matter to the attention of the minister is to obtain from him the view of the department, and a statement as to whether or not the department repudiates the letter which I have quoted. I may say that the minister has before him the letter and the correspondence to which I have referred.

The department has been in receipt of quite a number of complaints from homesteaders that they are being charged and have been charged for taxes against their homesteads prior to their receiving patents for the same. Some complaints have touched the point referred to in Mr. Pereira's letter regarding taxation of homesteads which have been abandoned,

and where the second homesteaders h^ve been billed for the taxes levied during the previous year. The question was submitted to the department, and I have a memorandum here, a portion of which I will read, which sets forth the view of the deputy minister on that point. The memorandum fn part is as follows:
In the first place, a few settlers have complained to the department that they were being' required to pay taxes which became due before they secured entries for the lands which they now hold. This appeared to us to be quite unfair, and it was decided to communicate with the Deputy Minister of Municipal Affairs at Regina on the subject. He now writes back that if a homestead has been abandoned or cancelled all arrears of taxes are written off, so that the next entrant is not required to pay these taxes. Owing to the fact, however, that there is always some delay experienced in finding out what entries have been cancelled, there are cases where the new entrant is served for the payment of taxes which he does not owe himself, but upon his malting proper representations to the rural municipality secretary, the matter is always satisfactorily arranged. It is not necessary to have to make any further inquiry so far as this feature is concerned because we are now put in a position to advise any person who may make a complaint to the department in this regard what course' he should follow in order to secure redress.
The department was not aware of the nature of the provinical law upon this subject; but, receiving so many complaints of this nature where the homesteader was charged with taxation with which he had nothing whatever to do and which had accrued prior to his making entry, a protest was entered with the proper authorities at Regina, and a satisfactory answer was received. So that now, when we receive similar protests from homesteaders, we shall know how to direct them to have this remedy applied.
The other point that has been raised, however, is of much wider scope, as it involves the power of the province to levy taxes upon unpatented lands. It would seem that in the past we have advised all persons who might be inquiring for such information on this subject that no lands which belong to the Crown in the right of Canada can be legally assessed for taxes by any provincial, municipal, school or other local organizations. It was this statement, coupled with the information contained in my letters to Mr. Cuttle and Mr. Bayne, which gave rise to the newspaper article which has been brought to your attention. As for the provincial law itself, it would appear that under the statutes of Saskatchewan the owner or occupant of any land within a rural municipality

or a school district is liable for the payment of the taxes assessed upon such land. If such taxes are not paid within the required time, they become a lien against the lands affected, and the same may be recovered by distress of the goods and chattels thereon. The law provides further that the land itself may through proper judicial procedure become the property of the municipality and be sold subject to redemption. I have never heard of a single case where a municipality has undertaken to sell an unpatented parcel of Dominion lands owing to the non-payment of taxes.
It is true, as stated in this letter, that the department has always made reply to homesteaders, who have inquired as to whether lands the title for which was in the Crown were subject to provincial taxation, that such lands were not subject to such taxation. I do not know whether the provincial law taxes the interest of the occupant or the land itself. I am not a lawyer, but I understand that if they are taxing the land as they would tax it if it had been patented and the title vested in the individual, that is not legal. That is the advice given us by the law officer of the department; and it -would seem probable that the provincial authorities take that view, inasmuch as they have not, up to the present time, enforced this Act, .that is, to the extent of distraining and selling the land. I was in receipt of a letter this morning stating-whether it was absolutely correct or not, I do not know-that the provincial Government are going to insist on taxes being paid on those lands the title to which is now in the Crown. However, the letter the hon. gentleman quoted from, sent to Mr. Bayne on the 16th of February, he will see, does not touch that particular point. It states:
Many letters have recently been received by this department from homesteaders upon lands in the province of Saskatchewan who complain of demands being made upon them for the payment of taxes which have been assessed upon Dominion lands before such homesteaders were granted entry therefor, respectively under the Dominion Lands Act.
The department points out that the point should be cleared up. It has been cleared up, and I should think that there should be no trouble in future with regard to it. But when the department has been asked whether lands the title to which is in the Crown, the patents not having been granted to the homesteaders, are subject to taxation, the answer has been given that in the opinion of the department they are not. I
understand that some years ago the Government of Manitoba recognizing this fact, did tax the interest of the holder, including improvement and stock, and made this taxation a lien. At any rate, looking upon that as a very important point, we have recently referred it to the Justice Department for an authoritative opinion.
What action is likely to be taken by the department in case of the receipt from the Department of Justice of an opinion in the line of the statements the hon. gentleman has made ?
We, should be guided by the Justice Department, but I should imagine we should have to have a test case in the courts if there were any contention to the contrary by the provincial authorities.

I presume no action would be taken by the Department of the Interior unless Dominion lands were taxed. Of course, the department must see to it that the homesteader gets a patent clear of incumbrances.
The hon. gentleman is familiar with the Saskatchewan Act. Does he know just upon what the taxes are levied ? Upon the land ?

Upon the interest of the homesteader. It is quite agreed that the land cannot be taxed so that the tax can become a lien upon the land; of course, if the tax became a lien upon the land, the land could be sold. [DOT]

Following out what my hon. friend from Saskatchewan has said, there seems to be in the answer of the minister, as well as in the correspondence from the department, the elements of a great many difficulties for the municipalities without probability of any good result. The necessity of taxation will, of course, not be disputed, and the interest that a man has in the land which he is occupying and using, and which he holds against all the world except the Government of Canada, must of course be admitted to be a very substantial, tangible and taxable interest. Both in Saskatchewan and in Alberta-certainly in Alberta-while it may be said that it is the interest of the homesteader that is taxed, and while as a matter of fact it is only the interest of the homesteader that is taxed, the taxation is levied on the area of the land. That is a single tax at so much per acre.
A flat rate.

Yes. It is understood to be a right and proper taxation of the homesteader's interest in the land. Of course, it is impossible for the municipality to collect the tax by sale of the land, but it is not impossible for the municipality to collect the tax assessed against the interest of the homesteader in the land by distress upon the homesteader's personal property, and therefore the tax has been collectable and has been acknowledged as a proper tax and as equitable in practice in both these provinces. I would impress upon the minister that to throw doubt in any way upon the legality of the procedure and practice which has prevailed is certain to create an enormous amount of trouble, and as to whether it will produce a good result or not I think there can be no question that it will not.
There is no doubt as to the necessity of the taxation; there is no doubt that the man who occupies .and uses the land and who, in effect, owns it against all the world,' except the Crown, .should pay his share of the burden of the community in the way of taxes. Any steps, therefore, that are taken by the Government to disarrange existing conditions must be to the detriment of the general welfare in the western country. I would very strongly urge upon the minister that if there is any reference to the Department of Justice of the question as to the legality of the taxation that has been levied, it should be a reference for an opinion or an authority that would confirm the practice that has hitherto been followed.
It has been one of the very great grievances of the settlers in those two provinces that under the arrangement that was made, not only with the Canadian Pacific railway, but with other raiway companies which were given land grants in those provinces which were not exempted from taxation by the Parliament of Canada, that by reason of the Government of that day not issuing the patent to the grantee, the railway company was able to avoid paying its fair share of the taxation of the country, lhat was a condition that prevailed during many years. It was finally remedied by the issue of all patents that could be issued to the railway companies. But it was a very great grievance, and it would be an equally great grievance if the undisputed ownership of the Government in the homesteaders' land should be used as a means of preventing the homesteader from paying his fair share of the burden of the taxation in the locality in which he lives. The

great object of getting homesteaders and getting settlers is that 'by their presence there shall be, for the convenience of the people improvement of the conditions as they exist, and that one set of people who are getting the advantage of these conveniences should be relieved from the burden of taxation while,the others should be compelled to carry the burden is essentially unfair. It will be understood that many homesteaders do not get their patents within three years of the date of their entry, binder the law a homesteader need not take his patent out for five years after the date of entry, and there are many occasions when it is not desirable even to insist upon that limit. It would be most unfortunate if the homesteader, by reason of his refusing to take out his patent, even after he had become entitled to it, should be relieved from taxation. I would respectfully urge the Government not to take any action that will lead to the idea that the present practice is opposed by this Government or that the Government would under any circumstances use its influence or authority to prevent the continuance of the present practice, within, of course, legal and proper limits.
I understand that there is a case now pending before the courts to test the legality of the provincial Act levying taxes on grazing lands the title of which is in the Crown.

That is a different question from the homestead lands; it is the homestead lands we have especially in question. In my judgment there is no question that the interest of the leaseholder in the grazing land should properly be taxable.
Can the minister tell us again what has been .submitted to the Justice Department and how the question arose?
The question arose in the department through the receipt of a great many .communications from homesteaders protesting against taxes being levied upon their lands.
Taxes payable by a former entrant whose patent had been cancelled, or by the present occupant?

Both. No opinion has been expressed by the department as to the legality of the taxation of the interest of the occupant, but they have expressed an opinion as to taxation of land when the patent remains in the Crown.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The House is not in Committee of the Whole, and therefore it is not permissible for the same member to speak more than once. The practice of rising over and over again calls the minister up so frequently that the rule is being abused rather than observed.
I had not spoken before, Mr. Speaker; I do not suppose you meant that for me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman first introduced some observations and asked a question. When a member has been on his feet he is presumed to have spoken, and after that he cannot, of course, speak a second time.

I asked the question merely that I might speak intelligently; 1 simply wanted to know how the question had arisen. With regard to the question which seems to have been originally raised in the letter written by the secretary of the Department of the Interior to Deputy Minister Bayne on February 16, namely as to whether the new entrant could be made liable for the taxes of a cancelled entrant, there can be absolutely no question about that. A new entrant is not liable for the taxes which have been imposed on a former entrant; that is as clear as it as possible for anything to be clear, and the letter written by Mr. Pereira, secretary of the Department of the Interior, was absolutely uncalled for in its substance as well as in its tone. This letter, which was written by a representative of this Government to a provincial Government-true, not political friends of this Government, but at the same time having the confidence of the people-was written in altogether too domineering a tone. I do not see how the minister can raise at this junction the question as to whether a homesteader is liable for taxes that have been incurred after he became an entrant. There seems to me to be no doubt about that matter. The minister said that his department received complaints and protests, and of course he knows the conditions, but it is strange that this matter should come up now for the first time. It seems to have been settled beyond peradventure for the last twenty years, both while the western districts were territories and since they became provinces, that the homesteaders are liable in this respect.
As to the question whether a man is liable for taxes in arrears on a cancelled
homestead which he has taken up afresh, the answer is, of course, in the negative. As to the question whether a man is liable for taxes on a homestead incurred after he himself enters for it, there is no doubt that the answer should be in the affirmative. As to the question to which the minister has referred, namely, whether grazing lands should be taxable, that is a different question, but there is no doubt that, as far as Canadian courts are concerned, the ruling will be that such lands are taxable. In the case of the Calgary and Edmonton railway companies versus the province of Alberta, it was decided by our Supreme Court that the liability exists. I may tell my hon. friend that judgment was Tendered this morning by the Supreme Court of Canada in the case to which he referred, that of Vermilion Hills versus Smith, the court holding that owners of grazing lands are liable for taxes. The case was carried to the Supreme Court at Ottawa only because the litigants desired to carry the case to the Privy Council. The Supreme Court of Canada has already declared *itself on that point of law.
I want .to read the letter written by the *secretary of the Department of the Interior, a letter which is-I will not say isaucy, but which was not one that the representative of one Government should write to another. I do not know who wrote it; perhaps the minister knows?
No, I do not; I presume the secretary. I know it was supervised by the law clerk.

It is a little high and mighty, nothing really terrible, but it calls on the provincial Government a little as a man might call on his office boy. It is as follows:
Ottawa, 16th February, 1914.
Sir:
Many letters have recently been received by this department from homesteaders upon lands in the Province of Saskatchewan, who complain of demands being made upon them for the payment of taxes which have been assessed against Dominion lands before such homesteaders were granted-

speechtext: I might say to the hon. member that that letter has already been read and was placed on ' Hansard ' a few minutes ago.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was informed by a fellow member that it had not been read. I shall do no more than make a comment on it.

Mr. Speaker, what I
read was an extract from a newspaper which did not contain the whole of the letter. It is possible that my hon. friend may wish to read the other parts. Another point which I wish to make is that there are two letters from the department, and I read only one of them.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may have misunderstood, but my impression was that the hon. member read the whole letter from the newspaper from which he was quoting.
I read the whole article, tout it contained only extracts from the letter.

The world would still
revolve even if the letter were read twice. I shall now read the whole letter:
Sir:-
Ottawa, 16th February, 1914.
Many letters have recently been received by this department from homesteaders upon lands in the Province of Saskatchewan, who complain of demands being made upon them for the payment of taxes which have- been assessed against Dominion lands before such homesteaders were granted entry therefor, respectively, uder the Dominion Lands Act.
These complaints have been brought to the attention of the minister, and it is considered that the practice complained of should be put a stop to at once. The assessment in such cases is the assessment by provincial, municipal, school or other local authorities of lands the title to which is in the Crown in the rights of Canada, and is, therefore, clearly illegal. It is also very unfair and discouraging treatment of the homesteader. Nothing can be said in support of the practice which besides being illegal and unfair to the settler, is not in the interests of the province of Saskatchewan in which nearly all the cases in question have arisen, and it seriously injures immigration to that province.
I am directed to request that the necessary action be taken by you to have this very objectionable and illegal practice stopped at once in the province of Saskatchewan.
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
(Sgd)
J. N. Bayne, Esq.,
Deputy Minister,
Municipal Affairs, Regina, Sask.
L. Pereira,
Secretary.
The writer does not say: Provided these stories are well founded a change should be made. He does not say:	Kindly look
into this at your convenience. He simply says:	I want this illegal, objectionable,
unfair practice stopped; it is against the wish of this Government and against the interest of immigration. You will notice the reason he gave. I am glad my hon. friend told me it was revised by the law clerk. He says the reason is that ' The title

to which is in the Crown in the rights of Canada.' That is no reason, and the law clerk or whoever revised it ought to know it. The title being in the Crown is no reason why the lands should not be taxable. The reason why they are not taxable, according to the first paragraph of the letter, is that the man who is the entrant now was not the entrant when the taxation was made, and that is what the letter should have said. There is no doubt that the title is in the Crown and is until the day the patent is issued, but that is not the reason why it is not taxable; if it is not taxable the reason is that the entry has changed hands. Therefore .1 say that the letter is not only a little lacking in courtesy and good taste, but lacking also in good law. The reply of Mr. Bayne is as follows:
Sir,-I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 16th ultimo, your file 1428986, the contents of which have been fully noted.
I desire further to call your attention to the fact that I am aware of no good reason for the tenor of your remarks, for since and even before this department was created we have instructions to all municipal officials, the fact that an entrant should not uc charged taxes on account of some previous entrant whose claims on the homestead was either abandoned or cancelled. Sometimes it transpires that the municipal secretary does not learn of the change in occupancy until he has mailed his tax notices, but I have yet to learn of one of these officials who has failed to promptly adjust his records and of deleting therefrom any erroneous errors, such as that which you describe, on his receiving proper information that the homesteader has either abandoned or cancelled his land.
The following is an extract from instructions which are in the hands of every municipal secretary in Saskatchewan:
' If a homestead has been abandoned or cancelled all arrears are written from the records in so far as they are held as a lien against the land. . . If a new entry is made previous to July 1, the annual assessment is charged, or after that date, the liability of taxation does not commence until the next year.'
The statement of arrears of taxes which you have in your office may contain certain amounts which should be cancelled in accordance with paragraph 3 of the manual of instructions, as some homesteads that have been cancelled or abandoned since the said statement was compiled. In case a homesteader protests to you against these arrears you may have him produce his interim' homestead receipt as official proof of the date of his entry. You can make a note of this number and date, adjust the records in accordance with paragraph 3 therein and then carefully return nim his interim homestead receipt.
' All protests against your tax notices should be carefully investigated and full consideration and explanation given to those desiring an equitable adjustment, avoiding, if possible, appeals to magistrates.'
Contrary to what your letter assumes this

department has been quite aware of the situation for several years and in every case where taxes are improperly levied against a homestead, the matter is equitably adjusted without friction and contention.
I am aware of no one attempting to either adopt or defend the ' practice ' which you describe, nor has any municipal official refused to act in accordance with the department's suggestions in placing the homestead taxes on a regular basis. Where temporarily, certain improper arrears have been shown on the tax notices, it has been as a result of lack of information.
I would be pleased to hear further from you in this matter.
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd) J. N. Bayne,
Deputy Minister.
L. Pereira, Esq.,
Secretary, Department of Interior,
Ottawa, Canada.
I have read those letters that it might be quite clear that the calling down the provincial Government of Saskatchewan received from the Ottawa Government was uncalled for, and I think it would be up to the department now to write a letter to the Government at Regina and rather express regret for the hasty letter written by the secretary of the Department of the Interior.
I am still in doubt as to how a serious question ever arose in the department as to whether homesteads are taxable, and this letter does not explain. Evidently there has been confusion as to whether taxes might be continued from one homesteader to another, but how the other question ever arose is a matter of mystery. The minister says he has letters complaining of that from homesteaders who were taxed as soon as they were on the entry. It is the first time I have heard of this, and I would like to see some of the letters.

The House in Committee of Supply. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Department of Justice-Living allowance for judge of Atlin district, B.C., $1,200.
Will the hon. minister explain why there is a living allowance for this particular judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This allowance has been made for a great number of years-in fact, ever since there was a judge in that district-on account of the expense of living there.

Do any other judges in
Canada get the same treatment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The judge of the Supreme Court, and the magistrates of the Yukon also get living allowances.

I do not propose to discuss this particular item, 'but I would like to ask if it is the minister's intention to increase the salaries of the judges of the province of Quebec this year? He is aware that the cost of living has gone up for judges as well as for other classes of people, and judges are forced to enter into social functions in which other people do not have to participate. It appears to me that the salaries of the judges in the province of Quebec, at least, are abnormally low, and I would urge increasing them in all parts of our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt the increased cost of living applies to judges as well as the rest of us. I have every sympathy with the judges, but I am not in a position to say at the present moment just what will be done in that regard.

I would like to say a
word or two in regard to the suggestion of my hon. friend the member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) in favour of increasing the salaries of the judges. I have in previous sessions spoken on this question, and if I now speak for our judges in the province of Quebec, I do not mean to set apart the claims of the judges of other courts in the various provinces; but it is because I am a member of the bar of the province of Quebec. I would like to lay before the hon. minister the case of the judges of the Circuit Court of Montreal, eoncernina whom the minister has, no doubt, received a memorandum. I will not recite this memorandum,	but I may	perhaps beallowed	to summarize	its contents.
The Circuit Court of the district of Montreal was established in 1893. It has therefore been in operation for twenty-one years, but its judges receive to-day exactly the same salaries as when the court was established- $3,000 a year. There is one exception, that of the Chief Justice, who receives a salary of $3,600 a year. There are five times as many people in the district of Montreal as there were twenty-one years ago, and the cost of living, in Montreal especially, has at the least more than quadrupled in that period. ' Why ' this memorandum asks, ' have the salaries of the Circuit Court judges remained at a standstill? ' For two reasons: first, because the Minister of Justice when he increased some years ago the salaries of the Circuit Court judges of the province of Quebec simply forgot the Cireuit Court jjudgesi *of the district of Montreal, being under the impression that the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal was under the same conditions as the Cir-

they would otherwise give? A man who is underpaid does not feel too well inclined to give a fair day's work. Of course, members of the House are sacrificing themselves on the altar of the country. But I am not speaking on behalf of the members -they can take care of themselves-but on behalf of the underpaid judges. I know that with some people this is an unpopular stand to take. Some people say that judges are soldiers of fortune, because they have been appointed for life. I have not been actively in the profession for some years past, but I have the highest Tegard for the administration of justice, and I say that if you do not give our judges a fair salary, you cannot expect to have the ablest men to administer justice. Remember, Mr. Chairman, while comparing the work of the Circuit Court judges of Montreal with the work of the County Court judges of Ontario, I do not wish to minimize the work performed by these Ontario judges. I am simply answering an objection that has been unduly raised time and time again in this House against the claims of the Circuit Court judges in the district of Montreal. The Circuit Court judge of Montreal administers justice in a district with a population five times greater than it was at the time of the creation of the court, and always with the same salary, though the cost of living has risen to the high water mark during the last ten years. Once more I beg the favourable consideration of the hon. minister, and I hope that, knowing the facts as he knows them, he will reach a right decision. There may be obstacles, but I would urge upon him to rise above such obstacles. Though on his side of the House he may meet some opponents, he will find compensating support on this side. I see my hon. friend from L'Islet (Mr. Paquet) and my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny). Will they not stand by me in this instance? Will they not admit that the judges of the Circuit Court of Montreal deserve better treatment than they have received heretofore?

I was glad to hear the
plea of the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) in favour of higher remuneration for the very onerous and important services rendered to the country by the judiciary. It is a matter of great regret, however, that the hon. member had not, while he had more influence in this Chamber, made as strong a speech on behalf of the judges as he has made to-day. I reifer to the time when the hon. gentleman was a power-

ful member of the Government of this country. Then his voice could have been much more effective than at present. However, he has made such a very strong plea that I am sure the Minister of Justice will take the matter into consideration. I wish to say a word on behalf of some of the judges of New Brunswick, particularly on behalf of the judge of Divorce and Matrimonal Causes in that province. The hon. member for Rouville, perhaps does not approve of divorce.
I will make this proposition: do away with divorce, and I will support an increase of the salary.

I am not sure that ttte
increase in salary would follow the abolition of the court. I would point out that this judge has very considerable duties to perform. Two courts a year are held involving as many as nineteen or twenty cases last year, necessitating the judge going to the city of Fredericton at very considerable expense. Yet the total remuneration he receives for this service is $500 a year. Compared with this the salaries of the Circuit Court judges of Montreal are princely. He is one of the Supreme Court judges, which helps out his salary to some extent. But there is no reason why he should perform this extra service and not be reasonably remunerated therefor. The judge of Admiralty in New Brunswick does not do a tithe of the work of this other judge to whom 1 have referred, but he has a salary of $1,000 in addition to his salary as judge of the Supreme Court. I would respectfully suggest to the minister that the salary of the Divorce Court judge be placed at $1,000 in view of the large amount of work he has to do-much larger than formerly on account of the increase of population, and perhaps on account of the modern tendency towards the severance of the marital tie.
There is another class of judges in our province whose salaries should be increased, the County Court judges, who correspond to some extent with the Circuit Court judges in Montreal-though not entirely. These judges have not the opportunity of increasing their stipends as have those in the province of Ontario, and their salaries have not been changed for many years, although the cost of living, as the hon. member for Rouville has pointed out, has greatly increased within eight or ten years. The result is that in some instances-I would not say in all-judges have done what, perhaps, is not quite the correct thing for them to do, they have sought to increase theiT incomes by holding circuits in

courts in other counties, holding chambers away from their places of residence when, perhaps, it was not entirely necessary, in order to increase their remuneration which is altogether too small.
This should not be permitted; but the temptation should be removed. I have heard of instances where judges have very considerably increased their salaries by this means. I think the judge should be paid a proper remuneration for his work, and that these additional means of adding to his stipend should not be permitted. I would ask the minister to take into consideration an increase of the remuneration not only of the County Court judges of New Brunswick, but also of the judge of Divorce and Matrimonial Causes.

The hon. minister is. of course, familiar with the fact that in the province of New Brunswick we now have two divisions of the Supreme Court known respectively as the Court of Appeal and the Court of King's bench. It is the duty^ of the members of the King's Bench division to attend to the work in chambers, and the judges of that court reside at different points in the province. The chief justice resides at Dorchester in the county of

Westmorland, two judges live in the city of Fredericton, and one in the city of St. John. I understand that the assignments have been made to the respective judges for work in the various sections of the province, and before we take up the item for the province of New Brunswick I would like my hon. friend to secure information as to the assignments for the present year. This information will have a very material bearing upon the question of the travelling allowances to be made to these judges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to getting the information for the hon. gentleman. but I would like to point out that I am not submitting any vote for travelling allowances; that is all provided for by statute. As to the assignments of the judges, that forms a part of the administration of justice which is under provincial control. As I say, I shall be glad to get the information, but it does not bear upon any item this committee is called upon to vote, nor could the House control it if they thought it was not proper.

I quite appreciate that; I am asking that the information may be procured because it may throw some light upon the question as to whether the judges should receive an increase in their salaries.	-
It is a well understood fact that in New Brunswick the number of divorce cases is, unfortunately, increasing year by year; and the work of that court has expanded to a degree that must be viewed as a misfortune, as far as the province is concerned. Yet we have to face those conditions, and I think that the judge of that court is entitled to at least the same salary as the judge of the Admiralty Court, whose work, instead of increasing, has very materially decreased within my experience. This matter has been commented upon in the past and it might have a very great bearing on the judgment one might exercise on the question whether or not the judges are fairly compensated if we had the information for which I have asked.

I wish it to be distinctly understood tnat in raising this question I was not in any way criticising the Minister of Justice because the salaries of judges were not raised. I am sure that the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), in speaking for increased salaries for judges, was actuated by the same motives as myself. We feel that in the administration of justice there is something different from what there is in the administration of other depart-

ments. The administration of justice is non-political in its nature, and it may help the minister in increasing the salaries cf judges, if he knows exactly what the wish of this House is. For that reason it is well that members on both sides of the House should give their views. I believe that the present Minister of Justice, who has had experience on the bench, would be willing to increase the judges' salaries. I really cannot, at the present moment, appreciate the difficulties in the way; but I can perceive that certain conditions may have arisen that may have delayed the matter. I wish to place myself on record as strongly in favour of the increase. As to the judges of the divorce courts I have absolutely nothing to say. In the province of Quebec we have no divorce courts; but, speaking generally for all the judges of my province, I know that a judge receiving $5,000 a year as a salary, after he has paid his rent, his life insurance and the education of his children, has no margin and is very often in debt. Therefore I want to encourage the increase in the salaries as much as possible.

The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has presented the case on behalf of the County Court judges of Nova Scotia so well that I need add little to what he has said. I would call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the memorandum presented by the County Court judges a few years ago on the occasion of their interview with him. It will be seen from that memorandum that two of the County Court judges particularly are referred to, one in Halifax and one in Sydney. They are perhaps the hardest worked judges that we have in the land. The others also have a great deal of work that perhaps may not strike the Minister of Justice as existing in that part of the country. The judges of Ontario, corresponding to a large extent te the County Court judges in Nova Scotia, have not as much work to perform as the County Court judges in Nova Scotia. They have to deal with not only civil but criminal cases, and in addition to that in case there is any contentious matter, in the Probate Court they have to sit as judges on it. And if the minister remembers the case presented to him at that time, it must have struck him very forcibly that the County Court judges of Nova Scotia have a great deal more work to do than the County Court judges of Ontario. Whatever objection there may be to raising the salaries of the judges in Ontario corresponding to our

County Court judges, I do not think that objection would apply so far as Nova Scotia is concerned.

I do not wish to say [DOT]very much about the salaries of judges.
I fully concur in what has been said by other hon. gentlemen. There is one thing about the allowance made to^ judges for travelling which I wish to bring directly to the attention of the minister. I brought this matter to the attention of the deputy minister, and he felt rather embarrassed as to what really should be the ruling. The minister knows well that what shall be assigned to any court is a matter within the legislative power of the provinces. They assign the subjects that go to the Supreme Court and to the County Courts respectively. Sometimes this Parliament assigns duties to judges of the different courts. There seems to be a rule in the Justice Department that even if a County Court judge goes to a remote section of his district to hold a court, unless the Department of Justice thinks he should be paid for going there he will'not be allowed travelling expenses. The County Court judge has nothing to say about it; he has to go. The provincial authority says he shall try a certain style of case, and he has to. go there and try it. It is rather a hardship on him that, after he has travelled and performed the duty which is imposed upon him by the legislature having a right to impose that duty on him, he should not be paid. Some duties are imposed on County Court judges that might be regarded as almost trivial. For instance, in our province there is an appeal from the assessment court, of the towns or districts to the County Court judge. The County Court judge is not obliged to hold a special court to hear that; he usually hears it at the ordinary sittings of the court; but if he were obliged to go to the different parts of his districts to hold courts for that purpose, I rather think he should be paid. That is one of the things that might be regarded as being not within the contemplation of section 18 of the Judges Act. But I wish particularly, to call attention to a very important class of trial which must be held by the County Court judge under chapter 72 of volume 1 of the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia which provides for the trial of election cases. The trial of election petitions in Nova Scotia, whether municipal or provincial, is governed largely by the same practice and the same law as the trial of
Dominion election petitions. In Nova Scotia, we follow, as nearly as possible, the legislation and practice .that applies to this House. Section 3 of chapter 72 says:
The court shall, subject to the provisions of this chapter, have the same powers, jurisdiction and authority with reference to an election petition and other proceedings thereon, as it would have if such petition was an ordinary cause within its jurisdiction.
That is one of the things I wish particularly to bring to the attention of the Minister of Justice. When a County Court judge is obliged, under the law of the province to go from the town in which he resides to another town to try a case, I think the fair interpretation of the Judges' Act is that he should be paid his travelling allowance. I fully concur in what has been said by other hon. members with respect to the propriety of increasing the salaries of the judges. One word more. I cannot understand why the chief justices of the different provinces should not be on precisely the same footing in the matter of salary. In New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, two provinces which I know very well, we have gentlemen of very high attainments occupying this position. They require a knowledge of the law equal to that of the Chief Justices of Ontario and Quebec and an equally high standard of ability, and therefore I think it is invidious to make distinctions in respect to salary between the chief justices of the different provinces. It is rather a reflection on the Chief Justice of the province of Nova Scotia not to pay him exactly the same salary as the Chief Justice of the province of Ontario. Whatever trouble the Minister of Justice may get into by revising the salaries of other judges, he certainly should not be found fault with for putting the chief justices of the different provinces on precisely the same footing.

Before the minister replies, I have one or two observations' to make with regard to the law relating to travelling allowances of County Court judges. According to the law as it exists on the statute book to-day, it would appear that a County Court judge leaving the town in which he resides to hold court in another town in the same county is not entitled to any living or travelling allowance. That law was passed at a time probably when County Courts sat in only one town in the county, when judges appointed to the County Court naturally, and perhaps necessarily, took up their residences in the shire town. But

conditions which have developed in the province of Nova Scotia in the last twenty years have made it necessary to establish County Court sittings in different towns of the same county, and therefore it does not necessarily follow that a County Court judge resides in the shire town of the county, but in some other town where sittings are held. Therefore, according to the interpretation of the Act-and I have no doubt a perfectly correct interpretation according to the wording of it-a judge who resides in the town where the sittings are held, if it does not happen to be the shire town, does not get a travelling or living allowance for travelling to and hotel expenses in the shire town. I do not think it was contemplated or ever understood that a judge should not be paid his reasonable travelling allowance whenever or wherever he might have to go in order to discharge his functions as a County Court judge. As I stated a moment ago, there are instances in the province of Nova Scotia where County Court judges who have to leave their own town to hold a sitting in the shire town, have not been allowed their travelling allowance. That refers to counties where there are two seats of a County Court within the borders of the same county. I wish the minister would direct his attention to that feature of the Act and have it amended, so that County Court judges may get their travelling allowance whenever they have to travel, under the provisions prescribed by the provincial Acts which regulate the service, in order to hold court.

' The hon. member for Kings, N.B. (Mr. Fowler), said a moment ago that the Minister of Justice was going to take into consideration the various demands made by the members to increase the salaries of judges. I want to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the particular case of the district of Three Rivers. I have listened to the very eloquent plea of my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) on behalf of the Circuit Court judges of Montreal, and I have also heard the plea by other members for County Court Judges. In the district of Three Rivers things have developed very rapidly, and the cases that are tried there are not of the ordinary commercial kind. They arise out of the fact that property has taken a sudden rise in value; titles are all mixed up, and we have lawsuits involving titles, water-powers, and all kinds of things out of the ordinary trend of litigation. The judges

in Three Rivers are more than overworked. If the judges in Montreal and Quebec ought to get $7,000 on account of the high cost of living, I say that it costs more to live in Three Rivers than it does in Montreal. And if you are going to put an increase of ' salaries on the ground of work done, I say the judges in Three Rivers do more work on account of the number of cases. I am satisfied that if the number of cases tried in Montreal were divided by the number of judges trying them, there would not be as many cases to each judge as there are to the judges in Three Rivers. Besides that, they have to perform all the duties of the Circuit Court judges of Montreal. There is a line of cases which my hon. friend from Rouville mentioned, which in Montreal cannot come up very frequently, but which do occur very frequently in Three Rivers, that is, appeals from the game laws. If a lumber jack or anybody else is sentenced by a justice of the peace for killing a moose, or for any other breach of the game laws, he can appeal to the Circuit Court, and in Three Rivers those appeals are very frequent. They try every kind of appeal there-appeals from municipal assessment under the school law-and election protests, not only municipal, and school, but federal. The judges often have to sit for eight or ten days in succession. I submit to the Minister of Justice that there is no reason why a judge in Three Rivers should not get a salary of $5,000. The argument cannot be successfully put forward that a judge in Montreal has to pay more for the necessaries of life than a judge in Three Rivers. You can buy the necessaries of life cheaper in Montreal than you can buy them in Three Rivers.
If the amount of work is taken into consideration, I am here to say that the work of the judges in the district of Three Rivers is far more difficult than that of the judges in the city of Montreal. In a place where -there are ten or eleven judges together their work is not as hard, and they have not the same amount of work, as where there are only two judges. Some of the judges have had experience in a case which can be drawn upon, greatly to his advantage, by a brother judge. Then, in Montreal the judges have their rooms in the court house, and they have the Bar Library at their disposal, whereas in the district of Three Rivers the judge has to buy his own library. Not having any university in the district of Three Rivers, we do not get any fees from the students

to read law or to be admitted to practice, and therefore our library is defective. The result of this is that our judges have to put their hands into their own pockets and buy books, which they do not have to do in Montreal or Quebec. In Montreal, as also in Quebec, the judges of the Court of King's Bench sit as a criminal court. In Three Rivers the Superior Court judges have to preside in the Criminal Court. We have of late had a lot of work in that line; there have been two or three trials for murder in which new trials were granted, and this involved a lot of work for the judges. In addition, the judges at Three Rivers have to sit as .a court of review. Here they are performing all the work that is performed in the city of Montreal by one class of judges-the judges of the Circuit Court. They perform the work of the judges of the King's Bench and they sit in the Criminal Court. In addition to that the judges at Three Rivers have to go to Quebec and sit as a court of review.
Is that too much work for the two judges of the Superior Court?

I am not complaining and they are not complaining, but if the judges, at Montreal and Quebec get $7,000 a yeaT, I see no reason why the judges at Three Rivers should not get the same. If you say that this difference in salary is justified by the high cost of living in these two places, I answer that you cannot live more cheaply in Three Rivers than you can in Montreal or Quebec. But, I repeat that the judges of the Superior Court have to .sit in the Court of King's Bench and hear criminal cases, and they have to sit as a court of appeal in Three Rivers to hear appeals from the acts and decisions of the municipal and school bodies, appeals from acts and decisions taken under the charter of the city of Three Rivers and of other municipal .centres throughout the district of Three Rivers. We must not forget that this district is developing very rapidly. You have in that district the city of Three Rivers, which has increased in [population from 13,000 to 18,000; you have the town of Grand Mere, which has a population of 5,000, and which is increasing very rapidly; you have the town of Shawinigan with all its important industries, and you have the new town of La Tuque, which is also developing very rapidly. New industries are going into these towns and cities, and the amount of
litigation at Three Rivers is increasing every day. As a result of this these country judges can never sit down at, night before their fire-places and smoke their pipes. They have a great deal more work to do than the judges in Montreal or in Quebec. These country judges have to expend a good deal more money in order to keep their libraries up than the judges of Montreal or Quebec, who have the advantage of the Bar libraries.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

By way of implementing the remarks I made 'before six o'clock, addressed to the hon. the Minister of Justice, and so that I may get from him a complete answer to all the requests made regarding the salaries of the judges, I will read to the House two petitions which I believe are in the hands of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, but which should be on ' Hansard.' By reading these documents I do not intend to be parochial or provincial. If I state a case for the judges of my own pro%'-inee, I do not intend by so doing to deprive the judges of the other provinces of whatever recourse they may have. I speak whereof I know most. I will read first the petition sent to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice by the judges of the Superior Court for the district of Quebec. The province of Quebec is divided judicially into two large districts, Quebec and Montreal, with subdivisions for smaller districts. The petition is as follows:
Quebec, November, 1913.
To the Honourable Charles J. Doherty,
Minister of Justice of Canada.
The undersigned judges of the Superior Court, of the review district of Quebec, in cooperation with the judges of said court for the balance of the province, respectfully represent :	, ,	...
That they are constrained, for, among other, the reasons hereinafter given respectfully to call your attention to the indemnity paid to them for their services; they are almost daily reminded by their experiences, that it is quite inadequate to enable them to live in comfort and in accordance with their station in life, without exercising too great economy; they must deny themselves such necessary luxuries as useful and helpful legal and literary publications, and, more important still, they are unable to adequately provide for the future of those who are dependent upon them.
The cost of living, as compared with a few years back, has almost doubled; incomes and salaries which were formerly considered an independence, are now quite insufficient to meet anything but the most ordinary expenses of living. Of course, we recognize this condition is not confined to judges ; it is so also in every walk of life; but judges' salaries have

I agree with my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that something ought to be done for the judges, especially for the judges of the Circuit Court of the district of Montreal. They are in a special class, as my hon. friend has said, being judges of ' the poor man's court.' The roll of that court is always congested; the work the judges have to do, the hours they have to devote to their duties, are certainly great in view of the salary that is given them. I believe that not very long ago a demand was made for an increase in the number of judges of this court from three to six; and you will observe, Mr. Chairman, that a fourth judge has been appointed on that Bench. If the work is to be done by these four judges-and everybody knows there is work for at least six judges-I think that is an additional reason for an increase in salary. I do not know whether the hon. member for Rouville has mentioned any figure. At present these judges are paid a salary of $3,000 a year. In my opinion, these four judges should be paid at least $5,000 a year. They certainly earn such a salary, and nothing less would be adequate for the duties they have to perform. I do not know whether the Minister of Justice is ready to announce what will be the policy of the Government in the matter, but I simply wish to join my hon. friend from Rouville to endorse absolutely the remarks he has made, and tn' ask the minister to take seriously into consideration the petitions that have been forwarded to him.

Mr. Chairman, I regret that the hon. gentleman who just resumed his seat (Mr. Lamarche) should have concurred in the views expressed by the hon. member for Rouville. I must say right away that I am wholly opposed to any increase of salary for the judges, because, to my mind, they are already getting too much for the work performed in the country's behalf.
the Superior Court judges of the district of Montreal are getting just now salaries of $7,000 or $8,000 per annum, and I was not a little surprised at hearing the memorandum of the judges of the district of Quebec which the hon. member for Rouville has just read to the House. When complaints are being voiced as regards the high cost of living on behalf of people who earn $7,000 per annum, it strikes me as something laughable. I admit that in the case of a poor workingman earning from $1.25 to $1.50 per day, the high cost of

living may be made a consideration towards obtaining an increase of his salary, but such considerations cannot be urged in the case of people earning from $7,000 to $8,000 per annum.
As a matter of fact are there not in the province of Quebec retired judges who get more as pensioners of the State than they earned while on the Bench?
That question was never taken up before the Canadian electorate, and I intend during the next recess of Parliament to carry on a campaign against the increase of such salaries throughout the province of Quebec, whatever may be thought of it by hon. gentlemen who belong to the profession. In this connection, I put both political parties exactly on the same plane; hon. gentlemen on either side are always ready to rise in this House and. defend the privileges of the upper set; they remain silent when the rights of the common people are in jeopardy.
We have in the province of Quebec fifteen retired judges; out of that number, three get $8,000 per annum, though they earned only $5,000 while on the bench. That makes $3,000 more per annum than during their term of office, that is to say, they get $3,000 more per annum for doing nothing.
How could it be otherwise, when we have as Minister of Justice a retired judge in person? Of course, it may be that the law makers who provided such increases had their own cases in mind. In 1905, the then Minister of Justice was Mr. Fitzpatrick. The .salary of the Chief Justice was increased to $12,000, and he was on the point of himself going over to the Supreme Court.
I was listening the other day to the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel) when he acknowledged that there were in his department poor people earning from $500 to $600 per annum as temporary clerks, for the past fifteen or twenty years; and he added that he did not see his way to granting them any increase. Besides, he said, if they are not content with that, there are hundreds of people who are ready to take their places.
Do you suppose, Mr. Chairman, that in the event of the judges of the province of Quebec resigning to-morrow, on the ground of insufficient remuneration of their services, it would be found impossible to replace them? I can assure you, Sir, that there are on the other .side of the

House some hon. gentlemen-I "have a certain number of them in front of me who, having deceived their electors at the last elections, would be very glad to slip into those vacancies. It would not take me a half-hour to fill in the gaps.
As for me, and I speak on behalf of the farming community which I represent here, I say that the latter class is unaware of all that is going on; and in this connection I may tell you of an incident which occurred in the course of my last electoral journey. I was addressing a meeting at St. Michael de Napierville, and in conclusion was pointing out the case of the hon. Minister of Justice, who is at one and the same time a pensioner of the State, Minister of Justice and member of Parliament. On these various heads, I told them, he is drawing three salaries. After the meeting some Conservative electors came to me saying: You have not stated the truth; the Minister of Justice can not be a State pensioner. I ascended the hustings once more and told them: Go and inquire from Mr. Patenaude, the local member for Laprairie (a staunch Conservative), and if he does not confirm what I have just stated to you, I undertake to give up my mandate. Those people would not believe me.
Now, I would like to know from the Minister of Justice whether he intends applying on my behalf to the Prime Minister for an opportunity to discuss the Bill I have on the Order paper in reference to the matter we are considering just now?
The contention is that there are not enough judges in Montreal; I know the reason, and I am going to tell you what it is. Our Montreal judges, like those in other parts, often suffer from slight headaches and travel for the benefit of their health. Several of them even cross over to Europe every year. While they are on such trips their salaries are by no means cut down. But take a poor customs officer, if he be sick two days in succession, he must show a doctor's certificate-which costs some money-to draw his salary. What I now state is a fact; many a time I have witnessed such things while I was sitting on the Government side.
I stated that a judge, even in the event of a six months' absence in Europe, draws his full salary. But that is not the whole story; should he be called upon to act as chairman of a commission of enquiry, or
to fill some other office apart from his judicial functions, he draws $50 per diem besides his salary as a judge which continues to run.
That is the kind of justice which is meted out to us farmers and workingmen.
I say that the time is near when we will show our resentment of such grievances.
Quite recently, in this House, when we urged cutting off the duties on agricultural implements, the objection was raised that we would no longer have sufficient revenue to meet tire expenditure incident on Civil government. To that I answer: Let us begin with the judges,, let us cut off, to begin with, the pension of the Minister of Justice-whom I see just now occupying a seat opposite. That pension amounts to $4,666.66. Mr. Chairman, that sum is surely equal to the net revenue of forty-six farmers in my constituency?
Let us now compare the pensions paid to judges in Ontario and in Quebec. Fifteen judges in Quebec are the recipients of nearly $100,000. In Ontario, one judge gets $7,000, two get $2,500 and one gets $.3,000. The comparison is greatly in favour of Ontario. I may add that the Ontario judges remain on the Bench until 83 years of age. Indeed, there are judges in that province who might have asked to be retired eight years ago, and who have not done so yet.
In conclusion, I shall once more inquire from the Government whether an opportunity will be given me to discuss in this House the Bill which I referred to a moment ago? Should the Government stand aloof in this connection, I shall undertake to myself go through the province of Quebec and discuss the question against any lawyer appealing to the electorate.

I wish to bring to the attention of the committee something that has been very strongly impressed upon the minds of the people not only of Canada but of all civilized countries. I refer to the desirability of doing away with courts of appeal. According to the principles of British law-civil, canon, and all the other branches of law-people are presumed to know the law; in fact one of the maxims of the law is that ignorance of the law excuses no one. Strange to say, however, when it comes to the bench the surmise is that as the judges may not know the law, wre had better provide a higher court. I say, follow out the principle that they are presumed to know the law, and let the
10.38

matter stop at that. If you want to do the poorer people of this country a favour, cut off these needless appeals. Where a matter of principle is concerned, let the public counsel, at the public expense, carry the case to a higher court for the general good of the community or of the nation, but the idea is wrong that the people, who themselves are presumed, by a very pleasant fiction, to know the law, should wade through a sea of technicalities and expense to a court of last resort when there is no scientific way of deciding the matter at the end or any other time. The whole thing is a matter of opinion from first to last. There are no axioms, there are not even postulates of law; there are simply experiences which have been put together, which form a certain sort of history and which we are supposed to profit by, but largely they are problematical and unsettled. We may study ancient law, modern law, international law, the law of evidence, the law of real property, and so on-and what is it ? It is nothing more or less than a sort of eruption of a great volcano; it is all confusion-the lava is running all over the community; it is hardening and becoming ossified. We call it the principle of law in some cases; in others we do not know what it is. This incongruity should be done away with. It is all a toss-up at any time. Tbss your copper into the air; if it falls head up, do not go to law; if it falls tail up, do-and you are just as likely to come out right in that way as in any other way; in fact, you are more likely than if you go on with an appeal. So that if you come to investigate the matter and look into the whole system of appeal, and its foundation, you will find that it is absolutely incongruous, inconsistent and illogical to the last degree; there is absolutely no sense in it. It is being perpetuated by the fact that the people do not know what else to do. Therefore, in default of somebody with a louder voice and more influence to make these things known, I have the hardihood to do so on this occasion. The day is coming when it must be done. I have already seen the influence of these things; I have already seen in more than one part of the British Empire that a tendency to cut off sources of appeal, divisional courts and things of that sort, is manifesting itself. Put good men on the Bench-I do not say that good men are not there now-put the best you have, pay them high salaries if you have to; it is the cheapest thing in the long run, but lessen appeals. Have men on the Bench who are like Privy Councillors in 
England. They do not take a year and a day to decide a case; they hear you in a few minutes; they decide promptly whether there is anything in your case, and they render judgment the next day. But, lessen the number of them. We know that the tendency is that the more profound you look the less you know and the longer you take to know it. I know this is a most momentous question; I know it may seem ridiculous to launch it in this way, but I am doing so in all seriousness. From the very earliest time when there were courts of law-in the Egyptian days, in the Grecian days and in the Roman days-we find this same thing cropping up: the necessity of repressing a multiplication of appeals because,. as I say-and this is the reason-you cannot arrive at any scientific solution of the question if you keep on appealing it till the crack of doom.
In the first place, I wish to ask a question of the hon. Minister of Justice. When a judge goes out to sit in his district, are his travelling expenses paid by the Government or by himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When he goes out to hold the court within the territory which is assigned to him, his travelling expenses are not paid by the Government. But should the Government send him outside his territorial jurisdiction, then he is recouped of his travelling expenses from public chest.

The-minister's answer does not supply exactly the information which I am in need of. My query is this: there is a judge appointed for the county of Ri-mousi. He resides in Quebec. Now, what I would like to find out is whether, in the event of his coming from Quebec to Ri-mouski to hold the court, his travelling expenses are paid to him by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As regards the question of the judges' residence, that is a point which is settled by the Provincial Act, and I do not exactly remember just now how Rimouski stands in that respect.

We sometimes hear it said that there is nothing new under the sun, and to-day we are witnessing the same old story of lawyers agreeing and acting as a unit when the proposal is made to increase the salaries of the judges. I am in almost every respect at one with the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) in the views he expressed.

I listened carefully to the remarks uttered on either side of the House in respect to the judges' salarie_s. It may be that in certain particular instances these gentlemen are underpaid, but in most cases judges receive not less than $20 per diem. As stated by the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville, almost every year judges take holidays, and though there are no data to be found in public documents regarding the matter, it does not appear that the least particle of the judges' salaries is deducted.
