Was a gentleman named O'Brien appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. Mr. O'Brien was appointed temporarily as one of the legal officers.
Is he the gentleman who was formerly law clerk of this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

What was his salary and
when was he appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His salary in the department was $5,000 a year. He was appointed on the 4th July and resigned on the 30th of September.

What were the conditions
under which he resigned from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He simply resigned.
He was superannuated, was be not?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The position he held
as law clerk was abolished, and the branch of which he had been the head was reorganized. The position being so abolished, he became entitled-I have not under my hand the section of the Civil Service Act which provides for this-to his superannua-* tion, which was granted him. During the time he held the position in our department he received no superannuation allowance, but simply the salary of his position.
Was his superannuation based on his salary as law clerk or on his salary in the Justice Department?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As law clerk.
What was the salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As law clerk he was not in my department, and I do not come supplied with information as to his salary; but the superannuation annuity he received by reason of being deprived of the position he

held-his being so deprived resulting from the abolition of the office-was based on the salary of the position he held as law clerk of the House of Commons.

Even if. the position of
law clerk was abolished, Mr. O'Brien bettered his position, for he was given another poaiton in the Department of Justice at a larger salary.
' Mr. DOHERTY:	So far as the Department of Justice is concerned, the explanation is very simple. Mr. O'Brien's position was abolished. In the estimates of the current year, passed during the last session, Mr. O'Brien's salary as law clerk was dropped. As it was found that certain work required to he finished, and the salary of the law clerk was not available for Mr. O'Brien, who was the fittest man to do that work, and he was temporarily appointed to that other office in order that the work might be done.

Was Mr. Gisborne not
appointed to the position of parliamentary counsel immediately after the session?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. At the time Mr. O'Brien was appointed, the deputy minister was absent on the business of the country. Mr. Gisborne was acting deputy minister. Although it had been decided that Mr. Gisborne was the most fitting person to be appointed parliamentary counsel, we could not immediately spare him from the department, and so he was not appointed parliamentary counsel until the return of the deputy minister from England. In the meantime the work to which I referred had to be done.

Even if Mr. O'Brien's
position as clerk had been abolished, it was replaced by the position of parliamentary counsel, and this amount of $5,000 which was voted for the position of parliamentary counsel was available to pay Mr. O'Brien. It was not necessary to give him an increase of salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Perhaps so, but there
was $5,000 available for the parliamentary counsel, and there was $5,000 available for the legal officer. The complaint of the hon. member for Prescott is that we called him legal officer; the salary was precisely the same. It was not intended that Mr. O'Brien should be appointed parliamentary counsel; it was intended that Mr. Gisborne should be appointed parliamentary counsel. What advantage would have been gained

by our calling Mr. O'Brien, in the interval of his temporary employment, parliamentary counsel at $5,000, instead of legal officer at $5,000 I am at a loss to understand.
Mr. Kl'TE: Was it really intended that Mr. O'Brien should do anything in the Department of Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was intended that
Mr. O'Brien should finish, as I said a moment ago, the work that remained to be done, in connection, it is quite true, with his abolished office of law clerk. But, the office of law clerk having been abolished, there was no salary for him.
As law clerk, he was getting $3,350 a year, ,and for the position to which he was promoted in the Justice Department he got $5,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But no salary was
available for the position of law clerk.

Why was he not given a
position at the same salary, $3,350, instead of $5,000 a year?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Because we had one
position vacant to which he could be appointed, and the salary attached to it was $5,000.

As a matter of fact, Mr. O'Brien was kicked out of the department of the House of Commons and kicked into the Department of Justice, and in the process his salary went up from $3,350 to $5,000 a year. He never did any work in the Department of Justice, and in addition to the increase of salary, they were generous enough to add ten years to his services during the short period that he was upon the pay-roll of the Department of Justice, and he was enabled to retire upon a superannuation allowance of $1,741.50, instead of $1,339. There was an investigation last year into the conduct of certain officials of the law branch of the House of Commons. That investigation was conducted by Mr. W. D. Hogg, barrister of this city, and Adam Shortt, one of the Civil Service Commissioners. I will read the part of the report which referred to Mr. O'Brien:
Taking- the officers of the law branch individually, we find that Mr. O'Brien is a painstaking and industrious officer. His knowledge in regard to parliamentary Bills, both public and private, gained by long experience, is extensive. His ability as a draftsman is very good, and his attention to the details of the work is also very good. His defects are: a want of ability to manage the branch as chief officer, his desire to change and alter any documents placed be-

fore him, no matter by whom drafted, his inclination to find fault with those under him, sometimes without fair justification, his irritability in dealing with these officers, and his excitability. He says a good deal of his irritability is caused by the incessant strain upon him caused by the incompetency of his assis-ants, for whose mistakes he feels himself responsible. Still, we think his defects, however caused, prevent his being a successful head of the law branch, although as an individual member of the staff he is capable of doing very good work.
Upon the report of this commission Mr. O'Brien was dismissed from the position of law clerk, but the hon. Minister of Justice, out of the goodness of his heart, felt that something more was coming to Mr. O'Brien. I am not sure whether his generous treatment of Mr. O'Brien was intended as an olive branch to be held out to the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). If that was the case, I regret to observe that it has fallen far short of accomplishing its object. Mr. O'Brien, according to the Civil Service Act, and according to his record in the House of Commons, was not entitled to the preferential treatment which [DOT]was accorded to him by the hon. Minister of Justice. Surely it was sufficient to superannuate Mr. O'Brien according to the terms under which he was entitled to superannuation, in view of the reason for dismissing him from office, without transferring him to the Department of Justice. As I have said, Mr. O'Brien's salary as law clerk was $3,350 a year. Upon the report of this special commission appointed to inquire into his competency and fitness to discharge his duties, he was dismissed, and he was pitchforked, if I may use the term, into the Department of Justice at a salary of $5,000 a year. I understand that during the two or three months tnat he drew his princely salary of $5,000 a year, he performed no service at all in the Department of Justice. He called there at the end of each month for his cheque, which was given to him in due course. At the expiration of the short term during which he was qualifying . for superannuation upon a basis of $5,000 a year, the Department of Justice was good enough to add ten years to his service.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely the hon. member does not want to mis-state the facts. He is quite mistaken in saying that Mr. O'Brien was superannuated from the Justice Department on the basis of $5,000 a year. Before this temporary appointment to the position in the Justice Department was made, the gentleman had been superannuated, in view of the abolition of his
office of law clerk, and his superannuation was fixed on his salary as law clerk. With that, the Department of Justice had nothing whatever to do; that was done by the department of the House of Commons, of which His Honour the Speaker is the head. All that the Department of Justice had to do with was the temporary employment of Mr. O'Brien to do the work that I have indicated.
And the basing of his superannuation upon the salary of $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon;, it is not based on $5,000 a year. The superannuation had taken place before he came into the Justice Department.

As I said a moment ago,
Mr. O'Brien's salary was $3,350 a year. Ten years' service was added, and he retired upon a superannuation allowance of $1,741.50, instead of a superannuation allowance of $1,339. So Mr. O'Brien is pensioned upon the taxpayers of this country to the extent of $402 a year over and above that to which he would be entitled in respect of the services he actually performed.

What part of the
county of Frontenac does Mr. O'Brien come from?

The interests of my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) are not limited to the boundaries of his county. The hon. gentleman has other interests throughout Ontario which far transcend any interest he has as the representative of Frontenac.
Thank you.

I repeat, Mr. O'Brien lost his position as law clerk by reason of the report of this special commission which was appointed to investigate the law branch of the House of Commons. It was well known during the last session that something extremely unsatisfactory existed in connection with the law branch-that certain complaints were being made from time to time as to the manner in which that branch was conducted. A condition of mutiny existed among the members of the law branch; so much so that Mr. Speaker was obliged to interfere to bring about something like peace in that important branch. A commission was appointed, and they found that Mr. O'Brien was absolutely incompetent to discharge the duties of his office as law clerk. Not

only that, but lie had a very improper disposition of interfering with Bills that were sent to him for his revision. In the face of that report it was necessary to dismiss Mr. O'Brien, and if Mr. O'Brien had received the ordinary superannuation to which he was entitled he would have had $1,339 a year. I say that in view of that report the Minister of Justice scarcely exercised the discretion in the matter of making appointments to his department that one would expect him to exercise. Surely the report of the commissioners did not indicate that Mr. O'Brien had any special qualifications to discharge duties in the Department of Justice at the increased salary of $5,000 a year. The whole thing is apparently a frame-up to enable Mr. O'Brien to draw a superannuation allowance of over $400 a year over and above that to which he would be entitled in respect to the services he actually performed. The question was put on the Order Paper by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy): In how many instances was time added to the service of civil servants so as to count in their superannuation; and the answer was that during the fifteen years of the late Government there was only one case where time was added to the service of a civil servant to enable him to draw additional superannuation; but since the present Government came into power, within a space of less than three years, three persons have been superannuated upon a fictitious period of service; that is in addition to the time actually served. I do not know what the conditions were in the other cases, but I do submit that, in view of the report of the special commission appointed to investigate Mr. O'Brien's case and the manner in which he discharged his duties as law clerk, the Government, or the Minister of Justice, if he is responsible for it, certainly did show a special favour to Mr. O'Brien in the treatment he received in respect of his superannuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let me attempt to make it quite clear that foT .all this heinous offence I am -entirely guilty, and my friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has not the slightest responsibility. But let me -point out that, in so far as the hon.
10	p.m. -member for Richmond is finding fault with the fact that Mr. O'Brien had ten years added to his period of service 'as law clerk for -the purpose of fixing the -amount to be paid to him as an annuity, that was no action of the Justice Department. I am not seeking to shirk

my [DOT] responsibility for the actions of this Government; but as the hon. gentleman has undertaken to distribute responsibilities, I want to s-ay that was not the action of the Minister of Justice. I would like to add that, in the opinion of the Minister of Justice, it was the mere appli-. cation of the law. If the hon. gentleman will turn to section 15 of the Superannuation and Retirement Act he will find that it is provided that:
If any person to whom this Act applies is removed from office in consequence of the abolition of his office for the purpose of improving the organization of the department to which he belongs, or is removed or retired from office to promote efficiency or economy in the Civil Service, the Governor in Council may grant him such gratuity or superannuation allowance as will fairly compensate him for the loss of office, not exceeding such as he would have been entitled to if he had retired in consequence of permanent infirmity of body or mind, after adding ten years to his actual term of service.
The hon. gentleman -says that the commission reported adversely to Mr. O'Brien. The commission found that Mr. O'Brien was painstaking, that he was remarkably capable for the actual doing of the work with which he was -concerned; but that he was irritable, that he did not get on with people under his control; and the commission went on to recommend the reorganization of the Law Department and the -appointment of an officer holding a rank totally different from that given to Mr. O'Brien. That report was acted on by the department charged with the matter, and when they came to determine what should be granted to Mr. O'Brien by way of superannuation, they applied the law as I have just read it. The Minister of Justice did not do it; but if he had done it he could not have done it in any way more exactly in accordance with the law.
Now comes the very head and front of all this offending; now -comes what I did- The hon. gentleman -said at one time that I did this, at another time that Mr. O'Brien was kicked into my office, and at another time that he was pitchforked in. If he came in in either of the two last-mentioned methods, I do not know that I am responsible for it. But he did not. In the report of the commission that found fault with Mr. O'Brien in other respects, we had the certificate that he was thoroughly qualified to do the work of putting the -statutes in proper order. That work was required to be done. The position which

he had occupied had been abolished. The other position was vacant, and he was appointed to that position to do the work. The hon. member talks about the princely salary of $5,000. Mr. O'Brien was appointed to the office fox a period of three months. Any one can figure out the amount of the difference between a salary of $3,500 and one of $5,000 for that time: it would be one-fourth the difference between those two amounts.
I do not want to discuss the findings of the commission with regard to Mr. O'Brien. Mr. O'Brien was an old servant, and even assuming that he had the faults that the hon. gentleman has read from that report, he had also the very high qualities which that report itself attributes to him; and, if it did happen that he got, by the accidental combination of one position having been abolished and the oilier one being the only one available, $400 more for that three months than he otherwise would have got, I do not think this country is so ungenerous that it will condemn us for not finding some method of preventing that combination of circumstances, bringing about that result.

I desire to place on record
the balance of the report signed by the two special commissioners:
Evidence was given before us by the Clerk of the House of Commons, Dr. T. B. Flint, and his evidence was corroborative of some of the statements made by the assistant law clerk and the secretary of the branch, to the effect that the law clerk, influenced either by his tendency to alter and amend documents that were placed before him, or by an exaggerated view of the responsibilities of his office, had on some occasions made amendments and alterations in Bills after Parliament had become seized of them, and without referring these amendments to Parliament for its sanction and approval. A number of Bills were placed before us in which these alleged changes had been made. This conduct on the part of the law clerk is no doubt wrong. It is evidence that Mr. O'Brien has not properly and fully apprehended the serious nature of the duties of the law clerk. He seems to have ignored the fact that when a Bill is once introduced into Parliament there should be no amendments or alterations to it, excepting with the approval of Parliament. Mr. O'Brien meets these charges of Dr. Flint and the other officers by saying that it had always been the rule in the Law Branch to make such changes in Bills as would express the intention sought to be conveyed by a Bill in proper parliamentary, language. He has cited to us instances of Bills in which the former law clerk made changes after they had received their third reading and maintains that in many cases the changes made by himself were so made only after consultation with those having charge of the Bills and to correct manifest errors. He believes it is one of the duties of the law clerk to make changes and
alterations in Bills which have passed the House, so long as such changes and alterations do not affect or alter the clear meaning and intention of the enactment. He says practically that some one must finally judge as to whether the alterations should be made or not, and that it naturally falls to the lot of the law clerk to be that judge, he further contends that in regard to minor and trivial changes, such as correcting the spelling of a word, making a change in a 'date where it was manifestly wrong, renumbering sections in Bills or such like alterations, he considers it as essentially part of the duties of the law clerk to make changes at any stage of the Bill, and that he would consider he was not doing his duty if he allowed such clear and manifest errors to remain in the Bill.
There can be no question that neither the law clerk nor any other person has any right whatever to alter, amend or vary a Bill, once it has become the property of Parliament, and particularly after it has passed the House. Mr. O'Brien has, we think, shown that in regard to the changes that have been made heretofore, nothing harmful has resulted in any of the cases referred to and brought before us. Perhaps on this question it might be sufficient to say, that whatever Mr. O'Brien may have done with reference to the making changes and alterations in Bills, was done under the impression that because such things had been done or permitted in the past, he was safe in following in the precedent thus established; and no doubt his conduct in this regard may also' have been due to his great zeal in seeing that the Bills were couched in what he thought was proper language, and contained no mistakes of any description ; and while we must not be considered as agreeing with his contentions in this regard, perhaps it might be sufficient to say that in future the law clerk, whoever he may be, should personally see that nothing of this kind is done at any stage of the Bill without the sanction of Parliament or of the committees thereof.
The Law Branch of the House of Commons is, we believe, the most important of all its departments, inasmuch as it deals with the laws of the country, in the making and publishing of which the greatest possible care must be taken. It is also .a department requiring considerable legal knowledge as well as skill on the part of its officers in drafting and revising Bills and other documents. It also demands from the law clerk a knowledge of the general laws of Canada, so that in drafting or revising Bills whether public or private, he may be competent to judge as to whether the laws of the country as they stand, are being entrenched upon or interfered with, and to be able to advise in respect thereto. While Mr. O'Brien is possessed of many of these attainments, we feel satisfied upon a review of the whole evidence before us, that he does not possess the qualifications necessary to manage and conduct the business of so important a department. We think that for the safety of legislation passing through Parliament, and for the harmonious working of the office, considerable reorganization should take place, and we therefore beg to submit the following suggestions for the consideration of Your Royal Highness in Council.
That is all of the report that has particular reference to O'Brien. The fact remains that
Flattering as it might toe to the hon. member, I did not say his 'influence;' I said his interest.

I do not know that I
altogether agree with my hon. friend, that it would be flattering as coming from him.
It is a matter of choice.

I might in courtesy
accept that, and agree with him that any compliment coming from such a distinguished man as himself would be flattering to any member of this House.
The hon. member

If the hon. gentleman
-will possess his soul in patience, he will get a little bile off his stomach before I get through. He has stated that the Minister of Justice did something in connection with this man O'Brien as a sop to me. I must confess that until this evening I was not aware of anything about O'Brien-whether he had been dismissed or promoted, or anything else. It was not a matter that interested me particularly; and, as I say, I was not aware of the facts until to-night. I do not know that the House has been especially enlightened in regard to the facts-I might emphasize the word ' facts '-by the hon. member for Richmond. The hon. gentleman speaks of this man O'Brien as being very irritable.
I did not say so. The report says that.

The hon. gentleman
read from the report, and endorsed that in the reading. But surely the hon. member for Richmond would not find fault on that score. He ought to appreciate a man's being irritable better than any other hon. gentleman in this House.

The Commission reported
that he was irritable.

The hon. gentleman is boiling over again. This Mr. O'Brien had been long enough in the service to learn by experience to do better. There again, I think this criticism comes with bad grace from the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman has been long enough in the House to learn by experience that a good many of the criticisms that he sees fit to apply to ministers of the Crown, when finally ventilated, prove to be of no account whatever. Yet, he does not profit by that experience. While in one breath the hon. gentleman is talking about the dismissal of Mr. O'Brien, in another breath he speaks about the superannuation of this gentleman being increased very largely. I am at a loss to know where I come into this. Am I responsible for the dismissal of this
gentleman, or am I responsible for the increased amount of money that was paid to him? In each particular, where do I come into this matter? Of course, I had nothing whatever to do with the removal of Mr. O'Brien from office or with any other matter connected with him. As the Minister of Justice has properly said, I had no connection with it whatever. I fail to see why the hon. member for Richmond saw fit to bring my name into it. I really cannot see that he was justified in doing so. The fact of the matter is that the hon. member for Richmond seems to feel the weight upon his shoulders of tackling every minister of the Crown, when his Estimates come up, in regard to dismissals. He has that complaint to make. He has a certain amount of this stuff to get off his chest, and he is going to get it off. If the minister of any department comes forward with his Estimates, it is regarded as an opportune time for the member for Richmond to get up and read sheet after sheet of foolscap in regard to the dismissal of some man from a lighthouse, or a post office, or some other position. He has prided himself on being the champion of all those men who have been dismissed from the service since this[ Government first came into power.
Up to the present time I have not observed that the hon. gentleman's influence has been so very great in so far as his criticisms are concerned. I think they have had very little result. If it has given the hon. gentleman any relief to get rid of his feelings and to make himself the special champion of the people who have been dismissed, very well. If the hon. gentleman wishes to do that, I suppose there is no person who has any right to prevent him from doing it. Far be it from me. I love to hear the hon. gentleman's voice. He has a delightful manner, a pleasant way of putting things, although at times he becomes a little irritable, as he is now, when he speaks of the case of Mr. O'Brien. I may say to the hon. gentleman that I have never asked any special favours of any minister of any department and what I have to say in regard to my department I shall say in this House in the future as I have in the past, and in doing so I shall endeavour to be fair with any department that I am referring to. I shall not be deterred from Saying what I have to say because of any allusion made by the hon. member for Richmond. It will have no effect upon me whatsoever.

Having regard to the rules
that govern debate in this House, I suppose that the only retort I am permitted to make upon the hon. member for Front-enac (Mr. Edwards) is the retort courteous. For that reason therefore and for that reason only, I will say to him that it will ever be to me a matter of extreme regret that I am unable to rise to that high elevation of intellect and conduct which have always characterized him since he became a member of this House. With respect to his rather unpoetic suggestion that my thoughts were coining from the region wherein are situated the digestive organs, I venture to say that he made that suggestion from the experience of his own characteristics. My thoughts do not come from my stomach, and I am rather surprised to learn that an additional source of intellect and light is possessed by the hon. gentleman.

With reference to this
case, we were told that there was some trouble in the law clerk's department and that the law clerk was found carrying a revolver to protect himself from some of his subordinates and especially from his first assistant whom I considered to be the most inoffensive man in the service. If the law clerk had not been such an offensive bigot I do not think lie would have found it necessary to carry a revolver to protect himself. An investigation was held. I was informed that the Speaker, aided by the Clerk of the House, commenced an investigation, and that when the Speaker found that he would have to find fault with the law clerk he abandoned the investigation, and called in a special commissioner, Mr. Hogg, K.C., and also the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Mr. Adam Shortt. They continued the investigation. They had to find fault with the law clerk although they made their report very mild; but they had to admit that he was guilty of very serious things, especially changing Bills. I submit that if he was guilty of these offenses he was not entitled to have ten years added to his term of service and by this means to get a larger superannuation. I do not know what the reason was that prompted the officials of this House to give him this large superannuation but I was told that if he had not got it there would have been trouble in the Orange lodges of the country. We all know that Mr. O'Brien is a prominent member of the Orange Association and that some of his relatives are high up also in 
the Orange Association and if lie was not treated as he asked to, be treated there would be trouble. I have to admit that I am compelled to believe that the ten years were added to his term of service and a large superannuation was given to him to pacify him and his friends.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to a statement made some months ago by the Lord Chancellor, Lord Haldane. Speaking at University College, in England, he made the statement to which I will refer. On the occasion of his recent visit to Canada he had been the guest of the Bar Association of America in Montreal, at which meeting he delivered certainly what is considered as a great oration. He made the statement that, after investigating the opinions of the principal judges and counsel of the Dominions, but especially of Canada, he had come to the conclusion that a desire was expressed of reforming the House of Lords. In order to make the matter clear, I might be permitted to quote the very language used by Lord Haldane. The despatch on November 5 to the Canadian Associated Press is as follows:
-London, Nov.	5.-The Lord Chancellor
\ iscount Haldane, speaking last night at University College upon the Legal and Political Unity of the Empire made some interesting remarks on the establishment of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as a movable Imperial court.
He said that recently he had given a good deal of thought to this subject and the other day when in Canada, he was struck with the feeling among those best competent to give authoritative opinion, that if any change took place they did not want to appeal to some new court outside the dominions. It was easy to talk about a new court of appeal but it was not easy to define in a way which did not entrench upon the just claims of the dominions across the seas to the self-contained.
Canadians valued appeal to the King in Council very much, and if anything was to he done to alter the judicial arrangement they hoped the foundation of appeal and form of the court would not he varied. He thought that was a very pregnant observation and probably one which all self-governing dominions would make. It meant that the dominions did not want to appeal to any court outside themselves. They regarded the King in Council as something not aside from themselves.
'Well,' proceeded the Lord Chancellor, 'both parties in the State agree that the existing second chamber must he reformed in a fashion that will make it impossible for it to he the supreme appellate court for England, Scotland and Ireland, and that when that comes we shall have to find a new appellate court. What can that be? I have an impression that it will work out so that presently we will have to think of it in this way, that this great link of empire will be further developed and that all appeals whether from countries form-

mg' part of the King's dominions outside these islands will be to the King in Council just as it has been proposed with Irish appeals in the Home Rule Bill.	.
4 That will involve certain changes. The work will be far too great for the Judicial Committee as at present constituted. Supposing that body were still more enlarged and an Act was passed enabling it to sit in more divisions than one. You see what an important instrument we should have for solving imperial problems. All appeals would then be taken in council and would be heard by the Judicial Committee, but the committee, instead of sitting in one division as to-day, would sit in several places, and as the King is president in each of the dominions and is represented by his ministers, and as the Privy Council is an imperial body containing the Chief Justice in most of the different parts of the empire, you have got at once a court which does not offend the canon which the self-governing dominions set up that " the Supreme Court should not be outside themselves."
' In this scheme,' continued Lord Haldane,
41 see the ready solution of the problem vexing the minds of many statesmen. Supposing we had a boundary case out in Canada. What would be more easy than to export members from London to go and sit as the King's Imperial Privy Council committee in Canada and deal with these things on the spot.'
In conclusion, the Lord Chancellor said the reform of transferring appeals to the King in Council as enabling the Judicial Committee to sit in the dominions would be a good step towards the solution of the problem of imperial notification.
I would rather hestitate before criticising any opinion emanating from such a highly respected authority as that of the Lord Chancellor of England; but my hon. friend (Mr. Doherty) will agree with me that in a matter of that far-reaching importance the old maxim, ' let well enough alone,' *should apply. I think that every Canadian -in this case I hope that I speak the mind of [DOT] every Canadian-is satisfied with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as it is actually composed and as it deals with present conditions. Many of us in this House, and many outside the House, especially of the legal fraternity, would probably look with great complacency upon the Supreme Court of Canada as the court of final resort. For my part, speaking for the minority in the Dominion, for the province of Quebec, I have no hesitation in saying that I am perfectly satisfied with things as they are. In all the cases which have affected the minority, and m all other cases, the Judicial Committee :of the Privy Council as at present constituted 'has always given a fair interpretation of the constitution of Canada and of the law of the various provinces. Therefore I contemplate with some fear any proposed change in that court. Probably my conservatism is the cause of
that fear. I admit that in constitutional matters I am somewhat of a conservative.
With regard to this proposed change, strange to say, the London Times, which is supposed to be the most formidable exponent of imperialism, is opposed to the scheme propounded *by Lord Haldane. I have under my hand a comment of the new scheme by the London Times on the morrow of the announcement made by Lo d Haldane, and I will read a few extracts from that article. You will notice that the principal suggestion made by Lord Haldane is the one which consists in importing members-when I use the word ' import ' I use the very expression of Lord Haldane himself-from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to the various dominions in special cases affecting those dominions. The London Times of the 7th of November, speaking of the foreshadowed changes in the position and constitution of the Judicial Committee, uses the following language:
But the predictions or suggestions of one who has not only thought much upon the subject but who must help to construct any amending measure, are likely to prove in the main true, especially if they are in accordance with a strong current of opinion. The Lord Chancellor was not, we must assume, indulging in academic speculations.
The reason I call the attention of the Minister of Justice to this proposal is that very suggestive phrase-he was not indulging in academic speculations:
It must be taken that he had in his mind probable changes which would have an important bearing upon the future of the empire. Never, probably, in modern times was the Judicial Committee stronger than it is; rarely has it commanded greater confidence than today. Lord Parker and Lord Sumner bring to it valuable elements. It includes two Scotch lawyers; several judges of distinction from oversea, among them Lord de Villiers and Chief Justice Griffith, have lately sat to hear appeals : and one may now look forward to the frequent attendance of some members of the Supreme Courts of the dominions. It is safe to say that the times when questions of consequence to the colonies and India were decided by one or two judges, perhaps with no special knowledge of the law to be administered, will not return. There is also, in the opinion of most lawyers, including those of our dominions, a distinct improvement in the character of the judgments, which generally show a clear recognition of the duty of the final court, not merely to decide a particular controversy, hut, by exposition of principles and frank and full discussion of problems, to give a lead and guidance as to the settlements of future disputes. Its business is not to stifle or evade real difficulties, but to settle them.
At the Imperial Conference some colonial delegates urged the fusion of the present two Courts of Appeal-the House of Lords and the Judicial Committee-into one Imperial Court. All were agreed that the appeal must be in
Currents of thought.

Yes, currents of thought -bearing upon this most important subject. Let me be very frank with my hon. friend. I think he is a patriot and would not for a moment impair our Canadianism. I cannot too often repeat what I said a moment ago that in these matters we should leave well enough alone. Let us make our Supreme Court as strong a tribunal as possible; let us make it a court which shall carry the respect and confidence of all Canada, and let us strengthen that court to reach that much-desired result.
I am bound to say that our Supreme Court is. a highly respected tribunal. With regard to the Judicial Committee of the Privy-Council, for Canadian litigants and for Canadian cases I do not know where any change in the present system of appeal would be useful. Various opinions have been expressed in the House with regard t >
this matter. To my great surprise the*hon. member for South York has expressed the opinion that we should do away with appeals to the Privy Council. I am not of that opinion. As a Canadian, and especiallv as a member of the minority in this House, I have ia great confidence in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and I am opposed to the changes which are so frequently dreamt of. With all due deference to the high authority of the Lord Chancellor, I do not believe in exporting members of the Judicial Committee to Canada cr Australia to sit in special cases. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is, to Canadians, the legal sanctum sanctorum- perhaps it gains in sanctity because of its distance. I do not believe that Lord Haldane would promote the much vaunted imperial unity by altering the status of the Judicial Committee. That the court should remain as it is presently constituted is the unbiased opinion of many not only at the bar but on the bench as well. Last year, I

queried my hon. friend in this regard and he answered me that he had not heard of any change, but now, a year later, we have the opinion of Lord Haldane after his visit to Canada which shows that he has had some grave conversations with high authorities on this side of the Atlantic. I would like to know if my hon. friend the Minister of Justice favours any such change. I expect him to state clearly, so as to dispel all doubts, that he does not contemplate any radical change, that the Supreme Court will remain as it is, and that, above all, our system of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council will not De altered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman's anxiety has not very much to base itself upon; at all events I shall be very happy to set his mind at rest so far as I can do so by saying that I have not suggested and do not contemplate suggesting any very revolutionary changes with regard to the appeal as it exists at present to the Privy Council. As the hon. gentleman fully knows, so far as the judgments of our Supreme Court are concerned, there is, properly speaking, no right of appeal to the Privy Council; His Majesty in his Council has the right to grant leave to appeal if he deems proper. I do not gather from what is reported here as having been said by the Lord Chancellor that he suggests that he received while in Canada the recommendation of any change in the appeal so far as Canada is concerned or so far as the dominions are concerned. Nor do I gather from what he said in this address, which was made at a college, and which does not at all lay down any settled opinion, that in going on to suggest how things might work themselves out, he purported at all, either in binding himself to any plan upon which he had decided or, still less, in dealing with those matters which might so work themselves out, to be reproducing or basing his remarks upon any opinions expressed to him in the Dominions or in Canada in particular. If the hon. gentleman will look carefully at what the Lord Chancellor said he had gathered from his interviews in this country, he will see that what he says he had gathered was that there was -no desire for an appeal other than the appeal as it now exists to His Majesty in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and that the dominions, so far as he gathered their impression, were averse to the establishment of any other court of appeal to which appeals should go from the dominions. If I follow his idea further, the suggestion of
modification, so far as I see there to be any, js in the first place a modification of the right of appeal within the United Kingdom, so as to make that appeal to the Judicial Committee. The only change affecting us which the Chancellor says he thinks might ultimately work out is the change by which the court to which pur appeal now goes by leave of His Majesty should, while remaining the same court, possibly in certain cases transport itself to the different dominions to hear cases. But I do not gather that His Lordship suggests that he gathered in his visit in Canada or his interviews with people in others of the dominions that there was a desire for modification in the constitution of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as it now hears appeals from the dominions. The despatch says of Lord Haldane :
The other day when in Canada, he was struck with the feeling among those competent to give authoritative opinion, that if any change took place they did not want to appeal to some new court outside of the Dominions.
I take this to mean they did not want to appeal to any court outside the dominions other than the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. (Reading):
It was easy to talk about a new court of appeal but it was not easy to define in a way which did not entrench upon the just claims of the dominions across the seas to be self-contained.
There is sometimes talk about a court of appeal as distinguished from the appeal to His Majesty in His Privy Council. The despatch goes on to say:
Canadians valued appeal to the King in Council very much, and if anything was to be done to alter the judicial arrangement they hoped the foundation of appeal and form of the court [DOT]would not be varied.
One would almost think that the Lord Chancellor had been conversing with the hon. member for RouviRe. The despatch continues:
He thought that was a very pregnant observation and probably one which all self-governing dominions would make. It meant that the dominions did not want to appeal to any court outside themselves. They regarded the King in Council as something not aside from themselves.
So far-and I think my hon. friend will agree with me-the Lord Chancellor purports to be giving the effect of the views he heard in Canada; now he goes on to make his own observations:
Well, proceeded the Lord Chancellor, both parties in the state agree that the existing second chamber must be reformed-*

Manifestly he is talking now about the affairs of the United Kingdom. (Reading):
-in a fashion that will make it impossible for it to be the supreme appellate court of England, Scotland and Ireland, and when that comes we shall have to find a new appellate court.
All this, of course, is in the United Kingdom.
What can that be? I have an impression that it will work out so that presently we will have to think of it in this way, that this great link of empire will be further developed and that all appeals whether from countries forming part of the King's dominions outside these islands or from these islands themselves, will be to the King in Council just as it has been proposed with Irish appeals in the Home Rule Bill.
In other words, what he foreshadows is changes in the system in the United Kingdom. My hon. friend would not suggest that that presented anything affecting us.
No. Read the next paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have it settled practically that for the Dominions the court is to be the same as it is to-day. (Reading):
That will involve certain changes. The work will be far too great for the Judicial Committee as at present constituted. Suppose that body were still more enlarged and an Act were passed enabling it to sit in more divisions than one. All appeals could then be taken in council and would be heard by the Judicial Committee, but the committee instead of sitting in one division as to-day, would sit in several places.
All I see suggested there is the possibility that the appeal, while it is an appeal to His Majesty in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, should be heard, for instance, in Canada. The court would remain the same, but instead of the litigants going to the court, the court would come to the litigants. I may say, to satisfy my hon. friend's legitimate curiosity, that, although I had some conversation with His Lordship upon the subject of these appeals, at that time no suggestion looking to the making of the Judicial Committee a peripatetic tribunal was made on either side.
I read this and took it to be-I think that the context shows it to be-only the throwing out of a suggestion that might ultimately work itself out, and not a conclusion resting at all on any suggestion coming from anybody in Canada. I think it is quite clear from the article that all His Lordship went home with as the impression obtained in Canada was that the [DOT]dominions, so far as Canada could speak for them, desired no appeal to any courts

outside, of those now existing, that we were satisfied with the appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as it how stands.
Taking that as his starting point and .dealing with the interests of the United Kingdom, in view of the changes taking place there, he foreshadows a plan by which our appeals would not cease to go to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, but the appeals from the United Kingdom would go to the Judicial Committee. As to how far it would be desirable that the Judicial Committee should come to the dominions in cer-
11	p.m. tain cases, while I am quite aware that the suggestion does not seem to have met with enthusiastic approval, at all events by members of the Bar generally, I am very far from being sure that it should be cast aside as not having very considerable value. I do not quite share the views of the hon. gentleman that our respect for the Judicial Committee is due solely to the fact that we do not see it at close quarters. I would like to believe that all the enchantment does not come from distance, and that their lordships could stand even a cioser scrutiny. From a practical point of view, while I would not like to pronounce myself absolutely on such a thing as desirable, neither would I be prepared to brush the suggestion aside as not being worthy of consideration. I think it is conceivable that there might be cases where it would be advantageous that their lordships should come into the country where they are called upon to judge and familiarize themselves with certain conditions which they may have difficulty in realizing at the distance at which they sit. I take it that no suggestion of any change is made so far as our appeals are concerned, save that possibly the Judicial Committee might come to this country to sit, and that last suggestion, at all events, is worthy of careful and respectful consideration. But so far as any apprehension in my hon. friend's mind that there are any changes being worked out in secret, either officially or unofficially, to which any member of the Government of Canada is a party, I can assure him he can safely disabuse his mind of that. I would not undertake, and I do not suppose my hon. friend will expect me, to detail whatever conversation I may have had with His Lordship; hut I may say that when he went home, as he said he went home, with the impression that in this country we were not desirous of any

*appeal to any court other than the Judicial Committee as it now stands, while I do not flatter myself that he included me at all among those authoritative persons to whom he refers, he went home with an impression which, if it was not I who conveyed it to him, is the impression which I would have endeavoured- to convey to him if I had been the party referred to.

Has a second judge been appointed for Renfrew county? My reason for asking is that I have had a good deal of correspondence against the Government appointing another County Court judge. They say there is not enough work for one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far there is no occasion for protest; the vacancy is still there.

I wish to ask a question with reference to the Admiralty Court in Nova Scotia. Some years ago an effort was made to give us a better Admiralty Court in Canada than we had previously had had, but nothing really came of it. An effort was made to enable us to issue writs in the county of Cape Breton where there is a great deal of admiralty work, and all I would like to say to the minister is that the machinery which has been provided for the court is very inadequate. When the minister would perhaps care to listen to what I have to say, I will deal with it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I shall be very pleased to listen to him now. I beg to apologize to the hon. gentleman for having been interrupted and I shall be very pleased to listen to the hon. gentleman.

It is quite unnecessary.
